name: Mali Empire
summary: A wealthy West African empire built on gold and trans-Saharan trade. Its ruler Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 became legendary.

knownFor.label: Mansa Musa
knownFor.note: His pilgrimage to Mecca with gold became legendary.

knownFor.label: Timbuktu manuscripts
knownFor.note: Scholarly manuscripts on science, law and religion.

location.value: West Africa: the upper Niger valley and beyond, from the Atlantic coast to Gao at its height. It was the largest empire in West Africa.

terrain.value: Savanna and the Sahel along the Niger River, which was a highway for trade.

climate.value: Sahel and savanna climate with a rainy season.

resources.value: Gold (the Bambuk, Bure and Galam goldfields; nearly half of the Old World’s gold by the early 14th century), salt from Taghaza, copper and kola nuts.

disasters.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

population.value: Not given in Wikipedia. Estimates are uncertain.

urbanisation.value: Timbuktu, Djenné and Gao were great trading and learning centres. The capital’s location (traditionally Niani) is disputed.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Trans-Saharan merchants and scholars moved between Mali and North Africa.

economicBase.value: Agriculture, plus control of the gold and salt trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Trans-Saharan caravan routes linking West African gold to North Africa and Egypt, and salt from Taghaza.

wealth.value: Famed for its wealth. Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage to Mecca (1324–26) reportedly caused inflation in Egypt.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold dust, salt, copper and cowries as money. Taxes on gold, copper and salt. Gold nuggets belonged to the mansa.

inequality.value: The mansa and nobles, free people (horon), artisan castes, and slaves (traded across the Sahara).

governmentType.value: A monarchy under the mansa, with a council (the Gbara). Conquered areas were run by military governors, and vassal kingdoms paid tribute.

keyRulers.value: Sundiata Keita (founder, c. 1235–1255). Mansa Musa (1312–1337). Suleyman (to 1360). Mahmud IV (last, c. 1590s–1610).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Mali Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026) (infobox); World History Encyclopedia, Mansa Musa I page (search excerpt): Mansa Musa ruled 1312–1337

succession.value: Hereditary in the Keita dynasty, but often disputed. A former slave, Sakura, seized power in 1285.

institutions.value: The Kouroukan Fouga, a charter traditionally attributed to Sundiata’s time, and the Gbara assembly.

stability.value: Strong under Musa and Suleyman. Weak and short reigns after 1360 ended its “Golden Age”.

eliteConflict.value: Succession struggles among the Keita family after Mansa Suleyman’s death (1360).

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry and archers. Arab sources claimed a standing army of 100,000 including 10,000 cavalry (probably exaggerated).

majorWars.value: The Battle of Kirina over Sosso (c. 1235). Later losses to the Tuareg (Timbuktu 1433), the Songhai, the Mossi and the Fulani. A defeat near Djenné (1599).

territoryChange.value: About 1.3 million km² in 1350, falling to 400,000 km² by 1500 (Wikipedia infobox).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Sosso, the Tuareg, the Songhai Empire, the Mossi and Morocco.

inventions.value: Sahelian mud-brick architecture (e.g. the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu, 1327).

scienceEducation.value: Timbuktu and Djenné became centres of Islamic scholarship. Mansa Musa sent scholars to study in Fez.

openness.value: Open to Islamic learning and North African trade, while traditional religion stayed strong.

communicationTransport.value: Camel caravans across the Sahara carried goods from the north; Timbuktu was the starting point for trans-Saharan caravans.

religion.value: Islam among the elite and traders, and traditional African religions among many people.

languageWriting.value: Manding languages. Arabic was used for scholarship and records.

artsArchitecture.value: Mud-brick mosques (Djinguereber), and the oral epic of Sundiata kept by griots.

socialStructure.value: Nobles, free people, artisan castes (blacksmiths, griots) and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Mande identity and the epic of Sundiata, still told today.

dailyLife.value: Round mud houses with thatched roofs; mud-brick mosques; millet, rice, fish and shea butter.

neighbours.value: Sosso, Ghana, the Tuareg, Songhai, the Mossi, Morocco, Egypt and the Mamluk Sultanate.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Islam and Mande language and customs across West Africa. The traveller Ibn Battuta visited in 1352–53.

colonisation.value: Expanded by conquest across West Africa.

riseSignals.value: Sundiata’s victory over Sosso (c. 1235), and control of the gold-salt trade as Ghana declined.

peakPeriod.value: The reigns of Mansa Musa (1312–1337) and Suleyman (to 1360).
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Mali Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia, Mansa Musa I page (search excerpt)

declineSignals.value: Weak rulers after 1360, the loss of Timbuktu and Gao, and the rise of Songhai and others.

outcome.value: Fragmentation. After the 1599 defeat near Djenné, the empire broke up around 1610 when Mahmud IV’s sons divided it. The Keita retreated to Kangaba. Sources disagree on the end date. World History Encyclopedia gives the Mali Empire as 1240–1645 and says a small western part survived into the 17th century before the Moroccan absorption in the mid-17th century.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Mali Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); World History Encyclopedia, Mali Empire and Map of the Mali Empire pages (search excerpts)

sources.value: Arabic writers (al-Umari, Ibn Battuta, Ibn Khaldun), Timbuktu chronicles, oral tradition (griots) and archaeology. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Gomez (2018).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. The capital’s location, many dates and army figures are uncertain, and oral tradition and Arabic sources differ. Second source: Wikidata ends it in 1670; Wikipedia’s lead gives 1610. Britannica (checked 6 Nov 2026) dates it from the 13th to the 16th century, founded by Sundiata c. 1235.
